transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Mbeki, thank you for coming in. I have asked my senior colleague to join us while we discuss your son's medication.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is everything okay? He seems a bit more lethargic than usual today.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There has been a mistake with the antibiotic we prescribed for him. The liquid medicine itself was the correct strength, but the oral syringe we gave you to measure the dose was calibrated for a different concentration. Because of that, your son has been receiving double the intended dose for the last three days.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Double? You're telling me he's had twice what he needed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct. He has received double the dose for three days. Does that make sense, or would you like me to explain that differently?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I follow what you're saying, but why on earth would that happen? I did exactly what the syringe said.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The syringe provided didn't match the bottle's concentration. It was a failure in the dispensing process.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My son is small. To give him double the medicine for three days... is he going to be alright? Is this poisonous?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We have reviewed the dosage, and while it was double the intended amount, it is below the toxic threshold for this specific drug. We believe he will be fine, but we need to monitor him.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can't believe this. I've already missed two days of work to bring him in. I can't afford to be away from my business any longer than I already have.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't think you do. I'm the only one running my shop. If I'm not there, I'm losing money. Now I have to spend more time here because of a mistake you made.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The most important thing now is to ensure he returns to the correct dose.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm just... I'm very worried. He's so lethargic. Is that because of the overdose?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Lethargy can be a side effect of the medication, but it can also be a symptom of the infection he is fighting. We need to rule out any other complications.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is just unacceptable. Who is responsible for this?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There were several steps in the pharmacy and clinic workflow where this should have been caught.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not asking about the workflow. I'm asking who messed up my son's medicine.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a system failure during the dispensing process.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're avoiding the question. Did you not check the syringe before handing it to me?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The process for matching syringes to concentrations was not followed correctly in this instance.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My son is the one paying the price for a process not being followed.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We need to move forward with a monitoring plan.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to know if he is safe.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: As I mentioned, the dose is below the toxic level. To be certain, I want you to bring him back tomorrow morning at 8:00 AM for a blood test to check his kidney function.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Tomorrow? I told you, I can't miss more work.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand the timing is difficult, but the blood test is necessary for his safety. You can bring him in, and then I will provide a formal medical note for your employer or your records to cover the absence.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Fine. What else?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You will stop using the current syringe immediately. I have a new, correctly calibrated syringe here for you to use starting with the next dose. I want you to call me directly at this number if he develops a rash or if the lethargy gets worse tonight.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what happens if the test comes back bad?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: If the results show any irregularity, we will admit him for a brief period of observation and hydration. But based on the drug profile, we expect the results to be normal.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can't believe I have to keep coming back because of this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will see you tomorrow at 8:00 AM for that blood draw.

H.justification: Resident allows the patient to finish turns and remains regulated under pushback, though pacing is somewhat brisk toward the end.

E.justification: Error named explicitly in the first turn using lay language, and comprehension was checked once ('Does that make sense...').

A.justification: No direct apology language used and responsibility was consistently deflected to 'system failure' and 'dispensing process'.

R.justification: Resident uses generic validation ('I understand') but does not name specific emotions or engage deeply with the patient's distress.

T.justification: Plan includes specific steps (blood test, new syringe), timelines (tomorrow 8:00 AM), patient role (bring son, call if rash develops), and prevention (correctly calibrated syringe).
